questions.q: What fundamentally distinguishes an AI agent from a simple chatbot?
options: An agent can only respond in longer paragraphs than a chatbot
An agent uses a larger language model than a chatbot
An agent can take actions in the world through tools and decide what to do next based on the results, rather than just producing one text reply
An agent never needs a system prompt
questions.explain: A simple chatbot maps an input to an output response; an agent is given the ability to call tools, observe what happens, and decide on subsequent steps, letting it pursue a multi-step goal rather than answer a single turn.

questions.q: In the classic plan-act-observe agent loop, what happens in the 'observe' step?
options: The agent ignores the tool's result and moves straight to the next planned step regardless
The agent stops running permanently
The agent picks which language model to use for the next step
The agent examines the result returned by the action it just took and uses it to decide the next step
questions.explain: The loop is iterative: after acting (usually calling a tool), the agent must observe the actual result — success, error, or new data — because that outcome, not the original plan alone, determines what it should do next.

questions.q: What is 'tool use' in the context of an AI agent?
options: Giving the model a defined function or API it can call, with structured input and output, so it can take real actions or fetch real data beyond its own text generation
Switching between two different language models mid-conversation
Increasing the context window so more text fits in the prompt
Formatting the model's output as markdown instead of plain text
questions.explain: Tool use means exposing external capabilities — like a search API, a database query, or a calculator — as callable functions with a defined schema, so the model can request them and receive structured results back.

questions.q: When are agents genuinely overkill for a task?
options: Whenever the task involves more than one sentence of output
When the task is a single, well-defined transformation that a direct prompt can already solve reliably, with no need for multi-step tool use or decision-making
Whenever the user is a first-time customer
Whenever the task could theoretically use a tool, even if a single API call would answer it directly
questions.explain: Agent loops add latency, cost, and failure surface (looping, wrong tool choices) that aren't worth it for a task a single well-crafted prompt or one direct API call already handles reliably.

questions.q: What makes a tool schema 'well-designed' for an agent to call reliably?
options: It has as many optional parameters as possible so the model has maximum flexibility
It omits parameter descriptions so the model infers them from context
It uses a single generic parameter named 'input' for everything
It has a clear name, tightly scoped purpose, and explicit, well-typed parameters with descriptions so the model can predict exactly how to call it
questions.explain: Agents choose and fill in tool calls based on the schema's name, description, and parameter definitions; ambiguous names or vague, untyped parameters lead to malformed or wrong calls, while a narrow, well-documented schema makes correct usage far more predictable.

questions.q: In practice, what should an agent do immediately after receiving a tool call's result?
options: Always call the exact same tool again with the same arguments
Discard the result and rely only on its own training knowledge going forward
Feed the tool's result back into its context so it can reason about it and decide the next step
Terminate the conversation, since one tool call is the maximum allowed
questions.explain: Tool calling is a round trip: the result has to be placed back into the model's context so the next reasoning step can actually use the new information, rather than the model continuing to reason blind to what the tool returned.

questions.q: Why does robust error handling matter specifically for tools called by an agent?
options: Tool errors should always be hidden from the model so it stays confident
A well-designed tool returns a clear, structured error the agent can reason about and recover from, instead of crashing the whole agent loop on a failure
Tools should never be allowed to fail, so error handling is unnecessary
Errors should be logged only, never returned to the model at all
questions.explain: Real tools fail — bad input, timeouts, missing data — and an agent that gets a clear, structured error message can decide to retry, try a different tool, or ask for clarification, whereas an unhandled crash or a silent failure leaves the agent stuck or misled.

questions.q: What problem does tool selection and routing logic solve in a multi-tool agent?
options: It decides, given the current goal and available tools, which specific tool (if any) is the right one to call next
It removes the need to define more than one tool
It randomly picks a tool to keep behavior unpredictable
It only matters when the agent has exactly two tools
questions.explain: As the number of available tools grows, the agent needs a way to match the current sub-goal to the correct tool rather than guessing; this routing decision, whether done by the model itself or an explicit selection layer, is what keeps the agent from calling the wrong capability.

questions.q: What's a key risk of giving an agent access to too many tools at once without good organization?
options: The agent becomes more likely to pick the wrong or a suboptimal tool, since its choice degrades as ambiguity between similar tools increases
The agent's context window automatically doubles
Adding more tools always makes the agent strictly faster
Tool count has no effect on selection accuracy
questions.explain: The model has to choose among all provided tool schemas at each step; more tools, especially overlapping ones, increase ambiguity and make it more likely the agent selects the wrong tool or misuses a correct one.

questions.q: What is the core idea behind the ReAct (Reason + Act) pattern?
options: The model performs a hidden reasoning trace before every single word without ever taking an action
The model interleaves explicit reasoning steps with tool actions, using each action's observed result to inform the next reasoning step
ReAct means the agent reacts only to user messages and never initiates a tool call
ReAct requires two separate models running in parallel with no communication
questions.explain: ReAct explicitly alternates 'thought' steps, where the model reasons about what to do, with 'action' steps that call a tool, then feeds the observation back in — this interleaving is what lets the agent adapt its plan based on real results rather than guessing blindly.

questions.q: What distinguishes a planning agent from a purely reactive one?
options: A planning agent decomposes a goal into an ordered sequence of sub-steps up front (or periodically), rather than deciding only one immediate next action at a time
A planning agent never calls tools
A planning agent has no memory of previous steps
A planning agent can only handle single-step tasks
questions.explain: Reactive agents pick the next single action based only on the current state; planning agents explicitly lay out a multi-step plan toward a goal (and often revise it), which helps with tasks that require coordinated, ordered sub-tasks.

questions.q: What's the main benefit of a multi-agent system over one large single agent for a complex task?
options: Multi-agent systems always run faster purely because more processes are running
It guarantees zero coordination overhead compared to a single agent
Specialized agents, each with a focused role and tool set, can divide a complex task and often produce more reliable results than one agent trying to do everything
It eliminates the need for any human oversight
questions.explain: Giving each agent a narrower responsibility (e.g., one that researches, one that writes, one that reviews) tends to produce more focused, reliable behavior than asking a single agent to juggle every role and tool at once, though it does add coordination complexity.

questions.q: In an orchestrator/worker multi-agent pattern, what is the orchestrator responsible for?
options: Performing every task itself while workers remain idle
Breaking the overall goal into sub-tasks and delegating them to specialized worker agents, then assembling their results
Storing the embeddings for a vector database
Replacing the need for any worker agents at all
questions.explain: The orchestrator acts as a coordinator: it decides how to split the larger goal into sub-tasks, routes each to the appropriate worker agent, and combines their outputs into a final result, rather than doing the specialized work itself.

questions.q: What does a 'reflection' or self-correction step add to an agent's process?
options: It has the agent critique its own intermediate output or plan and revise it before proceeding, catching mistakes earlier stages missed
It forces the agent to repeat the exact same output twice for redundancy
It disables tool use for the remainder of the session
It replaces the need for any human review permanently
questions.explain: Reflection has the agent (or a second pass of the same model) evaluate its own draft answer or plan against the goal, which often catches logical errors, missed steps, or incorrect tool results before they propagate further.

questions.q: Why does an agent need explicit state and memory management across multiple steps?
options: Because without it the agent can't retain earlier context, tool results, or decisions once the conversation grows longer than what fits naturally in a single turn
Because language models have no context window and need external memory to hold any text at all
Because state and memory are only relevant for agents with zero tools
Because it removes the model's need to read the current user message
questions.explain: As an agent takes many steps, relevant facts, prior tool outputs, and decisions accumulate; explicit state or memory management (like scratchpads, summaries, or external stores) is what lets the agent stay consistent instead of losing track of what it already learned or did.

questions.q: Why does human approval matter for certain agent actions, like sending an email or making a purchase?
options: Approval steps are only useful for actions that cost nothing
Because agents can misinterpret a goal or a tool result and take an incorrect but hard-to-reverse action; a human checkpoint catches that before it happens
Because language models are legally required to get human sign-off on every single action
Because approval steps make agents run faster
questions.explain: Agents can act on a flawed plan or a misread tool result; for actions with real-world consequences that are expensive or impossible to undo, having a human confirm the action before it executes is a practical safety net against that failure mode.

questions.q: What makes an approval checkpoint well-designed within an agent workflow?
options: It shows the human exactly what action the agent is about to take and its parameters, pausing execution until they explicitly approve or reject it
It approves every action automatically after a short delay
It hides the action's details from the human to keep the review quick
It only applies to the very first action in a session, never later ones
questions.explain: An approval checkpoint is only useful if the human can see precisely what will happen — the tool, the arguments, the expected effect — and the agent must actually block on that decision rather than proceeding regardless.

questions.q: What's the purpose of audit logging for an agent's actions?
options: To make the agent run more slowly on purpose
To create a durable record of what actions the agent took, with what inputs and outputs, so behavior can be reviewed, debugged, or investigated after the fact
To replace the need for any approval checkpoints
To store only the final answer shown to the user, discarding every intermediate step
questions.explain: Because agents make autonomous decisions, a detailed log of every tool call, argument, and result is what lets a team later reconstruct why the agent did what it did, whether for debugging a mistake or for compliance review.

questions.q: What's an effective way to prevent a 'runaway' agent from looping indefinitely or racking up cost?
options: Trust the model to stop on its own with no external limit
Give the agent unlimited retries so it never gives up on a task
Enforce hard limits, such as a maximum number of steps, a token/cost budget, or a wall-clock timeout, that force the loop to stop
Remove all tools from the agent entirely
questions.explain: Agent loops can get stuck retrying a failing action or spiraling through unproductive steps; explicit limits on step count, cost, or time give the system a hard backstop that ends the loop even if the model's own judgment doesn't stop it.

questions.q: Why are AI agents especially vulnerable to prompt injection compared to a simple chatbot?
options: Because agents ignore all text except the original user instruction
Because agents often read content from tools (web pages, documents, emails) that can contain hidden instructions, and an agent with tool access can act on those instructions with real consequences
Because agents never process any external text, only user input
Because prompt injection is only a risk for image-generation models
questions.explain: An agent that browses a page or reads a document may encounter attacker-planted text instructing it to take some action; unlike a chatbot that only produces text, an agent with tool access could actually execute that injected instruction, making the consequences far more serious.
